desc:
A warehouse stocks n kinds of goods. Every unit of kind i weighs weights[i] and is worth values[i], and exactly counts[i] units of that kind are available. A truck can load any number of units of each kind, up to what is available, as long as the total weight stays within capacity.

Return the maximum total value that can be loaded.

weights = [2, 3], values = [3, 5], counts = [3, 2], capacity = 10 -> 16   (two units of kind 1 and two of kind 0)
weights = [4],    values = [7], counts = [2], capacity = 9       -> 14
weights = [4],    values = [7], counts = [5], capacity = 7       -> 7
hints: Treating each unit as a separate 0/1 item works but creates up to 5,000 items. Can you represent "up to c copies" with far fewer 0/1 items?
Any number from 0 to c can be written as a sum of the pieces 1, 2, 4, ... plus one remainder piece. Splitting c = 13 into 1, 2, 4, 6 gives every count from 0 to 13.
Replace kind i by the bundles: a bundle of size m has weight m * w and value m * v. Run an ordinary 0/1 knapsack on all bundles.
editorial: The straightforward idea is to expand every kind into counts[i] identical 0/1 items, which can be slow when counts are large. Binary splitting keeps the expansion logarithmic: write c = 1 + 2 + 4 + ... + 2t-1 + r where r is the leftover so that the total is exactly c. Any number of copies between 0 and c is a sum of a subset of these bundle sizes, and no subset can exceed c.

Each bundle becomes one 0/1 item with weight size * w and value size * v. The standard downward 0/1 knapsack then finds the best load. There are at most about n · log(counts) bundles, so the time is O(n · log(c) · capacity). (A monotonic-queue technique can reach O(n · capacity), but binary splitting is simpler and fast enough.)
